strengths: Raises an important and under-examined assumption in mechanistic interpretability: causal interventions may create out-of-distribution representations.
Empirically illustrates divergence across several intervention families (mean-difference patching, SAE reconstruction, DAS) using EMD and PCA visualizations.
Introduces a useful conceptual taxonomy of harmless versus pernicious divergence, including hidden pathways and dormant behavioral changes.
Provides toy theoretical examples that concretely demonstrate how off-manifold interventions can activate silent ReLU units or create context-dependent behavior.
Adapts the Counterfactual Latent loss to regularize interventions along causal subspaces and shows promising reductions in EMD on a synthetic task.
The paper is generally well-organized and positions itself clearly relative to related work on activation patching and causal abstraction.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core concern that activation patching and DAS can produce off-distribution/null-space interactions is already known from prior work (e.g., Makelov et al. 2023; causal scrubbing; Zhang & Nanda 2024). The contribution is largely an incremental framing and a synthetic demonstration.

The empirical evidence for the prevalence of divergence is narrow: only a few intervention methods, layers, and models are examined, largely through qualitative PCA plots and EMD. There is no systematic benchmark across tasks or models, and no direct evidence that the observed divergence causes incorrect mechanistic conclusions in realistic settings.

The theoretical analysis consists mainly of hand-constructed toy examples rather than general results. The harmless/pernicious distinction is not operationalized, and the authors acknowledge that they cannot reliably classify pernicious divergence.

The proposed CL-loss mitigation is evaluated only on a synthetic grid-world MLP, not on any real neural network or language-model intervention task. This is a major gap given that the paper's motivation is mechanistic interpretability of real models.

The mitigation lacks comparison to natural baselines, such as projecting onto local manifolds/convex hulls, causal scrubbing, or other manifold-regularized counterfactual methods. The OOD evaluation uses an artificial partition of the synthetic data and does not quantify effect sizes or statistical significance in the main text.

The CL loss may bias intervened representations toward average natural latents, potentially weakening the intended causal effect or masking the very mechanism under study. The paper does not analyze this trade-off sufficiently.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence supports, e.g., that any divergence outside the null-space is potentially pernicious and that the method provides a path toward more reliable interpretability, despite only toy validation.

Reproducibility and practical impact are limited: no code or artifact release is mentioned, and the method is not tested on the standard benchmarks or models used by the mechanistic interpretability community.

strengths: Raises an important and under-examined assumption underlying causal interventions in mechanistic interpretability: that intervened representations remain on the natural data manifold.

The conceptual distinction between 'harmless' (null-space / within-decision-boundary covariance) and 'pernicious' (hidden pathway / dormant behavior) divergence is a useful framing that could guide future work.
Provides some empirical evidence that representational divergence is common across three different intervention families (mean-difference patching, SAEs, DAS).
The adapted Counterfactual Latent loss is a reasonable, if incremental, starting point for regularizing interventions toward the natural distribution.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core observation that interventions produce off-distribution representations and can activate dormant or hidden subspaces is already established (e.g., Makelov et al., 2023), which the paper itself cites; the paper does not clearly advance beyond this prior finding.

The theoretical analyses in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 are toy, hand-constructed examples rather than general results. The 'behaviorally binary subspace' formalism is informal, and the hidden-pathway/dormant-behavior constructions are simple linear/ReLU circuits that do not establish the phenomena occur in realistic networks.

Notational errors and inconsistencies undermine the theory: Section 4.1 introduces subspaces var_n and var_b in Equation 5 but the surrounding text refers to var_a, and the covariance argument is asserted rather than derived.

The empirical Section 3 is weak: a single model (Llama-3-8B) and single layers selected ad-hoc (e.g., 'we selected layer 10 as it had the lowest EMD difference'), no systematic layer sweep, and the baseline-subtracted EMD divergence measure is somewhat arbitrary.

The proposed mitigation is evaluated only on an extremely simple synthetic task (a 2D grid of 10 points with Gaussian noise and 64 noise dimensions), so it provides almost no evidence that the method would help on real interpretability problems.

No validation of the CL-loss fix on any real neural network, real interpretability benchmark, or actual pernicious-divergence case; the link between reduced divergence and reduced perniciousness is assumed rather than demonstrated.
The OOD improvement is small and on a trivial task, yet the abstract/introduction frame the work as 'a path towards more reliable interpretability methods,' which overstates the evidence.

The paper acknowledges it cannot classify pernicious vs. harmless divergence, which is arguably the central missing piece for making the framework actionable; without it the practical guidance remains vague.

Overall the contribution is closer to a well-motivated position/workshop paper than a competitive top-tier conference submission: the claims are plausible but the evidence is thin and the methodology is not rigorously developed.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexamined assumption in mechanistic interpretability: that causal interventions produce realistic counterfactual model states. This is a timely reliability question for activation patching, DAS, and related methods.

Provides concrete empirical examples of representational divergence across several common techniques (mean-difference patching, SAE reconstruction, and DAS), using PCA visualizations and Earth Mover's Distance to make the phenomenon tangible.

Introduces a useful conceptual distinction between harmless divergence (e.g., null-space variation or within-decision-boundary covariance) and pernicious divergence (hidden pathway activation and dormant behavioral changes), with toy circuit illustrations.

Adapts the Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss from Grant (2025) to operate on DAS causal subspaces and reports synthetic evidence that it reduces divergence and can improve out-of-distribution interchange intervention accuracy.
The paper is generally well organized, cites relevant literature, and explicitly acknowledges limitations and the preliminary nature of the proposed mitigation.
weaknesses: The core observation that interventions can create off-manifold/OOD representations is not entirely new; prior work has discussed related issues such as subspace patching illusions, causal scrubbing, and patching misinterpretations. The proposed method is an incremental modification of an existing CL loss.

The empirical divergence study is largely descriptive and not an apples-to-apples comparison: different models, layers, sample sizes, and metrics are used, and SAE reconstruction is not a causal intervention in the same sense as patching. It does not demonstrate that the measured divergence actually changes real mechanistic conclusions.

The theoretical analysis relies on hand-constructed toy circuits and informal examples rather than general theorems or realistic validation. The 'harmless' case in Section 4.1 uses confusing notation and assumptions, and the 'pernicious' examples are possible but not shown to occur in practical networks.

The mitigation is evaluated only on a very simple synthetic 2D grid/MLP task. There are no experiments on real transformers, nontrivial datasets, or actual interpretability claims, and no comparison to alternative regularization or manifold-projection baselines.

The CL loss constrains divergence along causal dimensions, but pernicious divergence can arise through hidden pathways, ReLU state changes, or dormant behavior in other dimensions. The paper does not directly measure or mitigate pernicious divergence, despite claiming progress on it.

The central claims that this offers 'a path towards more reliable interpretability' and mitigates pernicious divergence are stronger than the evidence. The OOD improvements are synthetic and modest, and the key failure mode of pernicious divergence remains largely unsupported empirically.

Reproducibility and experimental detail for the real-model divergence experiments are incomplete or inconsistent (e.g., layer selection versus averaging, no code link), and the manuscript has several notation/presentation issues.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexamined assumption in mechanistic interpretability: that causal interventions produce in-distribution counterfactual states.

Provides a useful conceptual distinction between harmless divergence (behavioral null-space) and pernicious divergence (hidden pathways and dormant behavioral changes), with formal definitions and illustrative examples.
Empirically demonstrates representational divergence across several intervention families (mean-difference patching, SAE reconstruction, Boundless DAS), which is a useful sanity check for the field.
Shows that a Counterfactual Latent (CL) auxiliary loss can reduce divergence in a Boundless DAS experiment on a 7B LLM while maintaining interchange intervention accuracy.
Introduces a modified CL loss that targets causal subspaces and reports improved OOD intervention accuracy on synthetic tasks, with an anti-correlation between training divergence and OOD IIA.
Includes an honest limitations section and acknowledges that the proposed mitigation is not a complete solution.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: prior work has already highlighted dormant subspaces, off-manifold activation patching, and misinterpretations of causal interventions (e.g., Makelov et al. 2023; Zhang & Nanda 2024; Heimersheim & Nanda 2024). The paper builds on these observations rather than providing a substantially new conceptual advance.

The theoretical results are simple and somewhat definitional. The coordinate-patching proof essentially shows that non-axis-aligned convex sets are not patch-closed, and the behavioral null-space analysis mostly restates that null-space perturbations do not affect the overall function.

The evidence for pernicious divergence is confined to handcrafted toy networks. There is no demonstration that common real-world causal interventions on LLMs actually produce misleading mechanistic claims due to hidden pathways or dormant behavioral changes.
The LLM experiment only shows that divergence exists and can be reduced; it does not show that reducing divergence improves the faithfulness or correctness of mechanistic explanations on a real task.

The proposed mitigation relies heavily on the existing CL loss from Grant (2025); the modification is incremental and evaluated only on a small synthetic MLP dataset with limited classes and noise dimensions. No comparisons to alternative regularization, manifold projection, or causal scrubbing baselines are provided.

Claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper suggests a path toward more reliable interpretability methods, but the practical utility of the modified CL loss for realistic mechanistic interpretability settings is not established. It also does not demonstrate that minimizing EMD reduces pernicious hidden pathways.

Some methodological framing is questionable: SAE reconstruction is not a causal intervention in the same sense as activation patching or DAS, yet it is grouped with causal intervention methods when measuring divergence.

The paper has notation and presentation issues, including likely typos in equations and sums (e.g., sum_{i=1}^{8} d_var_i), dense formalism that is not always clearly motivated, and insufficient experimental detail for the LLM CL-loss experiments.

strengths: Addresses an important and underappreciated concern in mechanistic interpretability: whether causal interventions produce out-of-distribution (divergent) representations and how this affects the validity of mechanistic claims.
The paper is generally well-organized and clearly written, with a logical flow from empirical demonstration of divergence, to theoretical taxonomy (harmless vs. pernicious), to a mitigation attempt.

The theoretical framing of behavioral null-spaces and the distinction between divergence that is harmless to a function's output versus divergence that is harmful to sub-computations is a useful conceptual contribution.

The synthetic examples in Section 4.2 (mean-difference patching activating hidden pathways, and dormant behavioral changes) are concrete and pedagogically effective, and the appendix hyperrectangle result is a clean (if elementary) characterization.

Applying the CL loss in the real Boundless DAS / 7B LLM setting and showing that EMD can be reduced while maintaining IIA is a useful sanity check, and the paper is appropriately candid about the limitations of its own mitigation approach.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core observation that activation patching and related interventions produce off-distribution representations has already been raised in prior work (Zhang & Nanda 2024; Makelov et al. 2023, which the authors themselves cite), and the null-space/dormant-subspace interaction is essentially the phenomenon described by Makelov et al. The paper largely systematizes and re-illustrates known concerns rather than introducing a fundamentally new insight.

The theoretical results are close to trivial. The coordinate-patching proposition reduces to the elementary fact that mixing coordinates of two points on a sphere can leave the sphere, and the appendix theorem (patch-closure iff product of projections, hence convex patch-closed sets are hyperrectangles) is a standard product-set argument. The authors acknowledge the proof is 'minimal,' and it is unclear that this rises to a publishable theoretical contribution at a top-tier venue.

The 'harmless' analysis is largely definitional/tautological. Defining harmlessness via the behavioral null-space amounts to saying that divergence is harmless when it does not change the function's output, and the paper explicitly concedes that an exhaustive characterization of harmless divergence is impossible and that harm is 'claim dependent.' This substantially undercuts the practical value of the taxonomy.

The pernicious-divergence demonstrations are toy-scale and hand-constructed. The hidden-pathway and dormant-behavior examples use tiny 2-layer networks with hand-designed weights and carefully chosen vectors; they establish possibility but provide no evidence that these failure modes actually arise in realistic models or affect real interpretability findings. No actual mechanistic-interpretability claim is shown to be wrong because of divergence.

The mitigation is weak and admittedly non-principled. The CL loss is taken from Grant (2025) with only a minor per-subspace modification; the paper itself states that minimizing divergence 'does not guarantee elimination of hidden pathways' and is 'not specific to pernicious divergence,' so the method does not actually target the failure mode the paper identifies as dangerous.

The empirical evaluation of the proposed modified loss is thin: a synthetic 10-class, 2-feature-dimension dataset with 16 noise dimensions, and an OOD regression with only 30 observations. The IIA/EMD trade-off in the LLM setting is essentially expected (the loss directly penalizes divergence), so it provides little independent evidence of utility.

Several divergence metrics (Local PCA distance, LLR, KDE) are introduced in the appendix but not connected to the central claims in a way that strengthens the argument, and the main-text evidence largely reduces to 'divergence exists' and 'a loss that penalizes divergence reduces divergence.'

The practical takeaways for the interpretability community are underdeveloped: the paper recommends reporting divergence and testing context-sensitivity but offers no concrete, validated protocol, and the concluding optimism ('many practical mechanistic projects can be satisfied by collecting sufficiently large intervention evaluation datasets') is not supported by experiments in the paper.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in mechanistic interpretability: whether causal interventions produce out-of-distribution representations and how this affects faithfulness.
Provides a clear conceptual taxonomy of harmless versus pernicious divergence, with formal definitions and illustrative theoretical examples.
Empirically demonstrates that divergent representations arise across several common intervention methods, including mean-difference patching, sparse autoencoders, and Boundless DAS.

Shows a practical mitigation path: applying the Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss to a 7B LLM Boundless DAS setting reduces representational divergence (EMD) while maintaining interchange intervention accuracy (IIA).
Introduces a modified CL loss that targets causal subspaces and provides evidence on synthetic tasks that it improves out-of-distribution intervention performance.
The paper is generally well-written, transparent about limitations, and includes useful appendices with methodological details.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the observation that causal interventions can create off-manifold or divergent representations is already known in prior work, and the theoretical examples are relatively simple toy circuits rather than realistic model mechanisms.

The central claim about pernicious divergence—hidden pathways and dormant behavioral changes—is supported mainly by hand-crafted theoretical examples; there is little empirical evidence that these phenomena materially affect real interpretability conclusions in large models.

The mitigation evaluation is narrow: the LLM experiment applies an existing CL loss to a single Boundless DAS tutorial setting, and the modified CL loss is tested only on synthetic MLP tasks. No real-world downstream interpretability task is used to show that reduced divergence improves faithfulness.
The modified CL loss requires access to known causal subspaces discovered by DAS and is not shown to address pernicious divergence specifically, only to reduce divergence magnitude.

Quantitative comparisons in the divergence analysis use different layers, models, and sample sizes across intervention methods, which limits direct comparability and weakens the empirical claim that divergence is equally pervasive across methods.

In the LLM setting, obtaining exact CL vectors required generating special token sequences containing valid counterfactual latents, raising questions about the practicality and scalability of the proposed mitigation.

Some claims, such as divergence outside the behavioral null-space being potentially pernicious, are stronger than the evidence provided; the practical harmless-divergence classifier is only approximate and is not empirically validated.

The paper does not provide a principled method for classifying harmful divergence for arbitrary mechanistic claims, as the authors acknowledge, leaving a significant gap between the diagnosis and the proposed solution.
